translations.text: I marveled with you, O lovers of Christ, because the new grace of the gospel was proclaimed through the Old Testament. My mind was enlightened with yours, for I saw the apostolic images illuminated by the words of the prophets. I acknowledge the grace, so that I may receive the reward. I saw new mysteries proclaimed through the old, when Abraham made his servant swear an oath at his thighs. He had him place his hand beneath his thighs and called the God of heaven and earth as witness to his words. He says, “Put your hand beneath my thighs, and I will make you swear by the Lord God, the creator of heaven and earth.” There is a great question in these words, for this was done because of the offspring who was to come forth from Jacob’s loins, in accordance with the saying, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins.” How can he be found to have sworn by [?]? For Isaac had been born long before, and the offspring had already come forth. When he administered the oath, there was no hope of any other offspring from the blessed man’s loins. It is clear that Abraham had within himself the life-giving seed, of which Paul said, “The promises were given to Abraham and his offspring.” He sets this out and explains it in the letter to the Galatians: “It was not said, ‘To you and to your offspring,’ as though referring to many, but ‘To you and to your offspring,’ who is Christ.” Thus it was shown that Christ is Abraham’s offspring according to the flesh, and he rightly administered the oath by that offspring. But the question is this: how did he administer the oath at his thighs, since the life-giving flower had already blossomed from him? Because that member had once become an instrument of holiness, and the divine offspring had once dwelt there, he therefore administered the oath by the temple. “Whoever swears by the temple,” he says, “swears by the one who dwells in it.” So also the Life-giver said concerning the Pharisees, “Woe to you, blind Pharisees, because you say, ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing, but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound.’ Fools and blind men! Which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? Therefore I tell you, whoever swears by the temple swears by the one who dwells in it.”

Just as a royal house that has once and [?] served as the king’s residence is called royal, even if the king moves away from it, because it was once dedicated to royal use, so too the patriarch’s bodily member, once it became an instrument of the dispensation to come, was a temple of the promised goodness. The oath was not in vain, but was a true testimony. Thus he administers the oath by his offspring and explains who that offspring is. “Put your hand under my thighs,” he says, “and I will make you swear by the Lord God, the creator of heaven and earth.” If this is so, Christ our Savior is the Lord and God of heaven and earth.

For the same reason, when various revelations appeared to the holy prophet Zechariah, there was one particular revelation of this kind. “I lifted my eyes,” he says, “and looked, and behold, there was a lampstand of solid gold, with seven lamps upon the lampstand, seven mouths for the lamps, and seven burning globes, and on its right and left were two olive branches. And I said to the angel who was speaking to me, ‘Lord, what is this?’” For what appeared to his eyes was one thing, while the interpretation that was to follow was another. The things that appeared did not signify themselves, but foretold certain other things. The prophet asks, “Lord,” he says, “what might this be?” If he were asking about what was plainly visible, then he would not be asking properly, if he did not know even what a lampstand was or what the olive trees were. Rather, the prophet seeks to understand not the visible things, but their interpretations. For he expressly says, “What might this be?” And the angel says to him, “Do you not know what this is?” And he says, “No, Lord.” With a humble mind he acknowledges his ignorance and learns from the truth.

He too was a brother to the eunuch who heard Philip say, “Do you understand what you are reading?” And with a humble mind he says, “How can I understand unless someone guides me?” Likewise, here he says, “Do you not know what this is?” And he says, “No, Lord. What are the two olive branches that are on the right and left of the lampstand?” And he explained the olive branches, and along with them, what the lampstand was.

Pay close attention. The lampstand stood in the middle, and the branches were on either side of the lampstand. But the angel explains that the branches stood not beside the lampstand, but before God, as though the lampstand were a figure of God—or, more precisely, of our Savior and his dispensation in the flesh. “Do you not know,” he says, “what these are?” And he says, “No, lord.” “These two branches are the two sons of abundance who stand before the Lord God of all the earth.” We must also pay close attention to this: he calls the lampstand seven-lamped because of the Lord’s dispensation in the flesh. Indeed, the lampstand was the Lord’s body itself, and it received the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit as an example for us, not because of any need of its own. As Isaiah also says, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall blossom from it, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him.” Which Spirit? Manifold in the effects of his working, yet an undivided gift in his nature. “And the Spirit of God shall rest upon him.” In the first words he speaks of the being of the Holy Spirit, for he also calls him the Spirit of God; in the words that follow, he calls the effects that he produces in others “spirit.” “The spirit,” he says, “of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and worship of God.” He speaks of the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit that rested upon the Lord’s body. The six-branched lampstand also depicts this. A lampstand is shown to make clear the illumination produced by the Holy Spirit’s works. To make this still clearer, a little further down he says, “These are the (seven) eyes of the Lord that look upon all the earth.”

Do you see that the seven gifts rested as an example [?] upon the Lord’s body for the illumination of all the earth? To make this still clearer, the evangelist bears witness: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” Where the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High were present from the very beginning of the divine conception, what need was there afterward for the seven workings of the Spirit? Yet the disciples of the heretics make the slanderous claim that only after his baptism did he become worthy to receive the workings of the Holy Spirit. We do not deny that the Spirit came then, but, as the evangelist himself says, “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descend and rest—he is the one.” “And I saw,” he says, “and I bear witness that this is the Son of God.” Do you see that he came to bear witness, not to supply any lack? Pay attention to how the truth explains itself by itself and has no need of human reasonings. “These,” he says, “are those who stand before the Lord of all the earth.” Zechariah calls the Savior the Lord of all the earth according to his dispensation in the flesh. Peter, the chief of all the apostles, was speaking with Cornelius: “We,” he says, “know the word that came throughout all Judea.” Of him it had previously been said, “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.” There he says, “The word that God sent to proclaim peace to the children of Israel: he is Lord of all.” He is Lord of those in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld, of the visible and the invisible. John speaks in agreement with him: “He who came from above is above all.”

But I also consider it necessary to refute the other objection of the heretics, who understand the apostle’s words with impious minds, as though he received his position above all as some reward for the cross—as though God exalted him because he endured suffering. They fell into this error because they neither read the apostle’s words correctly nor understood their force. “He humbled himself,” he says, “to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bend.” “Do you see,” they say, “that he was exalted after the cross? Do you see that he received exaltation as a reward for his sufferings?” But if he was exalted after the cross, why does John the Baptist proclaim, “He who came from above is above all”? He did not say that he would be above all, but [?], and not that he would be. The Savior himself also, while speaking with the Jews, said, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham came into being, I am.” For he is eternal, and he was, and he will be. You do not confess this, but we duly discharge our obligation to confess it.

From now on, let Christ’s glory and the Spirit’s exalted majesty be proclaimed; let the Father’s power also be proclaimed. Let the Only-Begotten also be exalted; let the Holy Spirit be glorified and praised. And let no one suppose that we are disrupting some order when we speak first of the Son, then of the Spirit, and then of the Father; or when we speak first of the Son and the Father, and then of the Spirit. For there is no ranking in the immortal nature. I say that there are no ranks, not because there is any disorder, but because there are no ranks of such a kind that one rises above another. For example, when I said that God is without form, this did not signify any ugliness, but that he has no bodily form. And when he is called without shape, it is not as though he lacks the beauty of a shape; rather, he is called without shape because he is incorporeal. Likewise, when I say that the divine nature is without ranking, I do not mean to indicate any disorder, but that there are no ranks there that contend with one another.

I spoke first of the Father, not as first in rank, but as conceived in thought; for he is the begetter of the Only-begotten and the root of the holy fruit. And since he is eternal light, the offspring of eternal light is eternal light. If anyone now dared here, in this assembly of the orthodox, where the correct confession of all knowledge is fully present, to name the Son before the Father in honor, would he not be criticized here by the orthodox? And now, would anyone dare to say to the church, “May Christ and his Father bless you”? Would he not create an impression of disorder, because he did not honor the root first and then the fruit? If someone said, “May the Son and the Father save you,” would it not seem to be some confusion, and would you not become angry because he was disrupting the order? But such opinions are not those of people who judge rightly, when someone looks to the truth and renders a just judgment, and brings forward the apostolic declaration in triumph: to mention, without distinction, first the Son, then the Father, and then the Holy Spirit. And listen to Paul, the great preacher. He writes to the Thessalonians: “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself,” he says, “and God our Father sanctify you.” He does not mean that the Son should sanctify first and then the Father. Rather, Paul’s clear and enlightened spirit wished to show that there is no such order in holiness: whichever is named first, the second shares his honor, and the third is neither diminished nor dishonored in any way. For this reason he also brings forward the names, because he knows the indivisible nature and the inseparable kingdom.

Let us ask Saint Paul: “Where did you find grounds to speak of God in this way, placing the Son before the Father—not in rank or power, but in words?” And now let us say: “Why did you mention the Son first and then the Father?” Let Paul answer, acting as his own defender and as the church’s teacher: “I say nothing on my own; Christ establishes such teachings through me.” For he himself says: “If you wish to obtain proof of Christ, who speaks to you through me.” If Christ speaks through me, do not criticize the Lord’s words, and do not find fault with his teachings. But can you not understand and believe that Christ speaks through me? Listen to him himself when he speaks in his own person. For if the names of the Holy Trinity stood under some [?] of subordination, and one was first in rank and power, another second, and another third, then the Life-giver would not have called himself Truth—“I am,” he says, “the truth”—and thus confused the order of truth. And listen again to the Life-giver: does he not speak first of himself and then of the Father? “If you keep my commandments” (Greek: “if anyone keeps them”), he says, “I and my Father will come” (and so on).

And since the heretics assign the Father a higher rank and regard the Son as a commander under the Father as king, let them now be asked: Would a commander dare to say, when speaking of royal matters, “The king and I will issue commands”? For we must understand what is above us from what is familiar to us. Would a created nature dare to place itself before the uncreated nature and count itself alongside the incomparable one, with whom it was not equal in rank, and say, “My Father and I will come and make our dwelling with him”? For by saying “I and the Father,” he made clear the distinction between the names, and by saying “We will come and make our dwelling,” he proclaimed the equal honor of their works.

Likewise, in another place, when the apostle Philip said, “Lord, show us your Father, and that is enough for us,” the giver of life answered, “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me, Philip?” He gives an answer contrary to the question. “Was it about you that I asked? Is it about you that I wish to learn? I say, ‘Show us your Father,’ not yourself.” And what does he say in reply? “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me?” If the Son is unlike the Father, how can the unlike one be known through one unlike him? Or how will you see the greater in the lesser, or the higher dignity through the lower, or the Creator through a servant? “I have been with you so long,” he says. He did not say, “My Father is with you,” but “I am.” Through my being with you, the Father is with you. “Have I been with you so long, and have you not known me?” He rightly said, “Have you not known me?” Philip says, “Show us,” and the Savior says, “Have you not known me?” He wished to show that God is not seen but known.

And he goes on to say, “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? And how can you say, ‘Show us your Father’?” This is instead of saying, “How do you expect to see him as someone else?” For if I am in the Father and the Father is in me, and the Son is known through the Father and the Father through the Son, how can you say, “Show us your Father,” as though you wished to leave me aside and see someone else? “I am in the Father and the Father is in me”—not as though their nature were something mingled, or as though one cup were inside another. He is not revealing any arrangement of bodily parts, but the intellectual meaning of the words.

“I,” he says, “am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” The Father is not known without the Son, nor is the Son revealed without the Father, just as thought is known through the word, and the word is revealed through thought. How can I know your thoughts except from the words you speak? Your words reveal your thoughts, and your thoughts give birth to your words. A person cannot understand words without thoughts, or thoughts without the words born from those thoughts. Likewise, the Father is known through the Son, and the Son is revealed through the Father. For this very reason the Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word,” to show his generation without suffering and to explain the unity of their essence. What the word is in relation to the mind, the only-begotten Word, God, is in relation to the Father. These very things are wonderful. I will repeat once more what has been said. Our earlier words were spoken for this very purpose: that from what belongs to us you might learn what is above us. While the word is still in the mind, it is invisible within what is invisible, intelligible within what is intelligible, incorporeal with what is incorporeal. When the word wishes to come out, it first moves forward into the mouth, and from there it clothes itself in sound—not as though it receives sound from another nature, but speech is articulated from the word itself. That which is invisible by virtue of its father’s nature clothes itself in sound and comes forth, becoming manifest to everyone, though previously it was hidden. As it moves forward, it fills everyone, yet does not depart from the one who begot it.

Who among human beings, when he speaks the word and teaches others, empties himself of the word and thinks, “Perhaps, when I put it into another person’s ears, I will leave my own mind bare and stripped”? Did not the word go out and remain there within? Did it not [?] many ears without departing from the one who begot it? Now, if a human word, when it moves outward and comes forth from the mind, is not separated from the one who begot it, would God the Word, who appeared in the world for our sake, leave his Father’s bosom empty? Away with that, you careless man! God forbid! For tens of thousands upon tens of thousands hear the word, and it enters countless ears without being divided. Rather, it is wholly with each person, entirely with everyone, and entirely in the mind. If the human word is entirely in the mind, wholly with each person, and entirely with everyone, how can they say of the Father that, if he begot, then an outflow and a severing occurred, and the indivisible was divided? Let the Giver of Life say to them, “Search the Scriptures.” Search them, and do not read heedlessly, but investigate the depths of their meaning through inquiry and examination. For God set the Scriptures before us and withheld the meaning of their sayings. He gave the Scriptures but did not lay bare their hidden interpretations. Rather, he left them as training in the racecourses of your endeavors, to exercise your mind and to see whether you would serve the Scriptures or do violence to them. In the same way, God set nature before us and hid the art. All materials and substances were set before us [?], and art arose in human minds. So it is also with the Scriptures.

And to make my words still clearer, God provided the natural substance of stones, not a finished building. He gave wheat; he did not make bread and set it before us. He gave grapes; he did not himself turn the grapes into wine. He gave wool; he did not himself make clothing. He gave gold mixed with earth; he did not himself separate it from the earth. Why? Because man was made in the image of God, he shares in the work of creation: God makes things and gives man the task of shaping them through craftsmanship. For example, he involved man, whom he made in his image, in the task of naming created things. He himself, as Creator, brought them from nonexistence into existence, and commanded his image to give them names. Likewise, he himself supplied the materials and entrusted the shaping of the work to craftsmanship. Who first fashioned a plow to cut through the earth with wood and iron and open a furrow, to make a yoke and traces, and to harness oxen for work with yoke pins? Wood and iron existed, but craftsmanship was nowhere among them. Who showed you, O man, how to fashion a plow in this way, or that the hard substance of iron could be softened by fire? Who showed you the methods for sitting and hammering such a thick mass and making a tiny needle? Who put it into your mind to make [?] and locks, or to prepare beams and roofs for houses? He says, “You ask a very foolish question. I have God as my instructor within [?], and you ask where I learned!”

And so, brothers, everywhere this human nature, resembling its Lord, adorns natural things through craftsmanship. If it keeps within bounds, the image is good; but if it goes beyond its bounds, it is dishonored by its excess. Here is an example. Man learned to drive the ox, train the horse, tame the camel, and the other animals that were given to serve us. But through greed he also learned to make other mixtures contrary to nature, mating an ass with a horse, which was not according to God's will. For in the beginning God said, “Let the earth bring forth four-footed animals and creeping things according to their kinds.” Greed devised other mixtures contrary to nature. Therefore God, to punish this excess, made these acts of human greed infertile. That is why a mule does not reproduce: it is not among those that, when they came into being, heard, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.” Nevertheless, he allows his image to do whatever it wishes, so that he may show its power, punish its excess, and reveal its pride.

Again, an immeasurable desire occurred to him to make an image in human form. “Let me imitate,” he says, “God, who made the image of man, and let me make an image of the body.” And through art he forces nature. Since he heard that God took soil from the earth and made man, his art falls into uncertainty, because it cannot truly imitate its Lord, and thereafter it resorts to devices and expedients. He gathers roots and flowers to prepare the colors. He makes eyes like eyes, but they do not see. He measures out ears, but they do not hear. He polishes the nostrils, but they do not smell. He roughens the mouth, but there is no voice on its lips. He fashions the shape of the feet and thighs, but the feet neither walk nor take steps. For in this way God makes it clear that he allowed his image to do whatever it wished, but not to exceed its limits, lest it become proud and fail to recognize nature, or its own freedom and salvation. Yet, since he learned that man was created from the earth, “I wish to imitate the Lord and Creator through another art”—the art of physicians. When he sees decay in the body, he puts an iron instrument to work and cuts away the decayed part. And when he wishes to dig into the wound, to bring it to [?], and to restore the eaten-away flesh to its proper measure, he is not a creator who can create it anew. What art, then, can the image practice to imitate its Lord? He turns to the soil from which the body was created and prepares medicines and poultices from it. With one he removes the decay, and with another he rebuilds, and thus he fills up what is lacking in the body.

And see the wondrous things: how God sits and watches as though watching his children. And what does this watching reveal? Not that he might learn, but that he might train them. Thus the source of all good things instructs his image. As at the beginning, God set before Adam all the wild beasts, livestock, and birds, to see what he would call them—not so that the All-knowing One might learn, but so that he might train his image. The very desire to devise things reveals the useful applications of building, carpentry, shipbuilding, metalworking, and weaving. Moreover, looking at the stars is not an idle activity. Rather, observing the arrangements of the stars is useful to sailors, as is paying attention to the stars in the east and recognizing a favorable time for sailing—not to construct horoscopes, nor to introduce myths of fate and fortune [?], but to follow the Lord’s words: “Let there be lights in the heavens, and let them shine upon the earth, and let them serve as signs, and for days and seasons.”

So that you may not suppose that the image discovers the means of doing everything by itself, blessed Solomon makes this clear in a single statement. “He gave me,” he says, “knowledge of everything that exists: to understand without error the structure of the world and the arrangement of created things; the beginning, end, and middle of times; the cycles of the elements and the orders of the stars; the habits of animals and the fury of wild beasts; plants of every kind and the powers of roots. Whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest, whatever is visible and whatever is invisible, I came to know,” he says, “as a human being,” instead of saying, “as the image.” And how? He says, “Wisdom, the master builder of all things, taught me.” But she taught you what is measurable, not what is immeasurable. See how far the art has spread and advanced into the immeasurable! It looked at human nature, and the image of God considered how the mouth’s instrument of speech was constructed. It observed nature and, through art, made something resembling nature, devising a mechanism with many pipes joined together and intermingled with one another. And see what art does to imitate the work of the master builder! It constructs bellows for me, which do not have breath of their own, but by giving and receiving, opening and closing, take in outside air in turn. Then, from the two bellows, it sends the breath into wind-bearing nozzles, and from there into every [?]. It understands that, even if the breath moves, no musical note is produced. It devises a means for this too: arranging it with the fingers, it plays melodies. And where did you get this, O human being? How did you learn to construct bellows that receive air, and to arrange the filtered air into melodies with your fingers? “You ask very foolishly,” he says. “Did I not already say that I am the image of God? I looked here at my own nature and made something resembling it. For in me they see an incoming breath from outside, and my coverings, repeatedly opening and closing, receive the air mingled with everything. I see that two little tubes give and receive the air, as though through a kind of funnel, through [?], into my mouth. I see that air enters, yet there is no speech unless the tongue, moving between them, arranges the sounds. I looked at myself and made something resembling my own nature, and through myself I personally came to understand the Lord’s art. As David also says, ‘Your knowledge became wonderful in me.’ I looked here at myself and glorified the master craftsman. I imitated my Lord and, through art, plainly depicted my nature.”

The harp is not something evil, but it became an instrument of filthy songs. If it sang divine praises as it did at first, it would not be defiled. Although such instruments are causes of unrestrained desire at revels, nevertheless, if an instrument were dedicated to God as it was at first, it would not be evil or defiled. As David also says, “Praise the Lord with psaltery and lyre, with strings and harp, with cymbals, with sweet sounds, with praise, with drum and dances.” Now, if it were not used in revels of debauchery, nor again in the worship of idols, but through the very thing by which someone learned the art he also offered fruit to God, the knowledge of the art would not deserve blame, if he acknowledged the Lord. The lyre would not deserve blame if someone offered songs to God with the lyre. Therefore blessed David did not sing filthy songs with the lyre, but offered sacred praises to God and put the demons to flight. When the evil spirit afflicted Saul, the Scriptures say that David played the lyre, and Saul found relief. Do you see that every art has been fashioned to please God? There would be no evil if everything were done according to God’s will.

What, then, did I intend to show when I turned from speaking about God to such matters as craftsmanship and the image’s resemblance to its Creator? I intended to set forth the Lord’s words and expose the heretics’ groundless opinions. The Lord’s words? Which ones? “Hypocrites,” he says, “you know how to interpret the appearance of the heavens.” You know the crafts and understand their principles, yet do you insult the master craftsman of all things? Through your craft you have imitated your Lord and made whatever you wished, for you were established in the image and likeness of the Creator. Yet do you proclaim that the Creator is unlike the one who begot him? I freed you from your subjection to sins, yet do you call me, who am Lord of all, into subjection? “Yes,” they say, “because it is written that the Son will be subjected.” We have already spoken about this to the best of our ability—or rather, by the power of God, for these words are not ours but God’s. Remember them. Nevertheless, even now let us direct a brief rebuke at them. Let us examine the statement. In the world to come and at the resurrection, when you say that the Son will be subjected, will you not become a sun and an angel? “At the resurrection of the dead,” he says, “men do not take wives, nor do women become wives of men, but they will be like angels.” Will you then rise above your present rank, while the Son descends from his lordship to a lower position? Have you not heard Paul? “Creation,” he says, “was subjected to futility,” and “creation itself groans and suffers birth pains until now.” Creation—that is, heaven and earth and everything else—was subjected to the futility of human beings. For he calls humanity futile because it has marred the image and descended to the likeness of animals. Thus elsewhere he says, “Vanity of vanities, everything is vanity,” and David says, “Every living human being is altogether vanity.” So creation was subjected to humanity, which had marred the image. And how was it subjected? The sun rises upon the unworthy, rain falls, springs flow for the ungrateful, and the earth bears fruit for those who show no gratitude. In this way creation was subjected to futility, and not willingly. For if it had been a matter of its own will, it would not have submitted to the unworthy, but it was because of the one who did not subject it in hope. “Creation itself,” he says, “will also be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the Son of God.” But if creation will then be freed, will the Son enter into slavery?

Examine the Scriptures, and do not slander them. Examine them, and do not search aimlessly. Examine them, believe, and do not contradict them. Where did you learn to say, “Did the Son exist and was he begotten, or did he not exist?” Where did you learn that begetting and making are the same? Did Peter teach you this, or did Paul declare it, or did the giver of life hand it down? Read the Scriptures. Moreover, you do not stand by what you yourself say. For the very moment you ask whether he existed and was begotten or did not exist, you speak falsely, because your question is not about what you confess. First confess that the Son was begotten, and then ask about existence and nonexistence. But you deny the facts and make the words [?]. If you do not grant that he was begotten, why demand an investigation of it? “Did the Son exist,” he says, “and was he begotten, or did he not exist?” First grant me that he was begotten. First seal a written acknowledgment that he was begotten, and then inquire how. But you deny the nature and subject the words to investigation and inquiry. You say that making and begetting are the same. Yet for me too they are not the same unless the character of both is first made clear and their meanings then agree. For if I say that looking and seeing are the same, one thing will be expressed. But if I say that hearing and seeing are the same, then I seem to have assigned to hearing what belonged to the eyes. And where did you learn that, for God, making and begetting are the same? For if you confessed that he was begotten and made, then you could properly say that they are the same. But if you never confess that he was begotten, how can you consider begetting and making the same? You will be found not only to introduce empty words, but also to be entirely devoid of truth.

And now we must learn why the heretic cleverly argues that making and begetting are the same. For God, he says, is a simple and diffuse essence, unlike us: we beget with one set of organs and work with another, since we beget with our reproductive organs and work with our hands. God is not like that, but is simple and diffuse and without form. In the same way that he begets, he also makes. Now, since you promise to explain the characteristics of invisible things, puffed up with your misplaced cleverness, I will show you from visible things whether works are performed in that same way. Bring visible hands into the discussion, so that through visible things the evidence concerning invisible things may also be brought before us. For the hand itself is one and the same, whatever it does, but its work is not called one and the same, nor does it display one and the same action. For example, with this one and the same hand I built and demolished. Are the two the same? For they also say that we beget in one way and work in another. I too say, following the same example, that we build and demolish with the same hand; we strike and smooth with the same hand; we push, throw down, and raise up those who have fallen with the same hand; and we count and cancel the count with the same hand. Now, are building and demolishing the same? Or striking and smoothing, and the other actions, each in turn? Are these not the words of fools and absurd tales? Would not Paul’s mind groan at this? Would not Peter be angry at such words being mixed into the teaching? Have you renounced Christ and begun learning what others teach? Have you not heard him who said, ‘Whoever is ashamed of me and my words, I too will deny him’? For many, many times I confess Christ but am ashamed of his words, just as you yourself will feel regret when you come to discussions about God and hear the name of the Father and of the Son, and are ashamed of the words. Then you say such things as, ‘Did the impassible one really beget? Was there any begetting at all? And if that is so, it was by an outflow and a division.’ Do you see that you are ashamed of the words? It is to people like this that he says, ‘Whoever is ashamed of my words, I too will deny him.’ Oh, the folly! They became hunters of words alone, not true examiners of realities. This vanity, guilty before the Lord, has ruined and corrupted everything.

What I have said many times, I will say now as well: the heads and leaders of these heresies are known, and the holy Church has never accepted heretical teaching. If you can ever recall that someone of such-and-such a name became the founder of the Church’s religion, you must bring him forward. But I know that you cannot identify the person who introduced this sect—what you call a sect, though it is not a sect but the truth, which the apostles themselves preached from the beginning. After them, the Council of Nicaea confirmed the same thing, so that it would be evident that this was the worldwide and universal faith. Among that great multitude of bishops assembled in one place, only seven bishops did not agree, and those outcasts and rejected men were cast out. The whole world agreed, for they were of the apostolic, well-seasoned blend.

And see these wonders: this whole new world became like the old covenants. Just as Abraham, who was most faithful, armed his three hundred and eighteen servants born in his household and drove away the five kings of the Assyrians who had come against the land of the Palestinians, so Christ, following the same pattern and number, gathered to himself three hundred and eighteen bishops to wage war against the heretics. Abraham took three hundred and eighteen servants born in his household and went against the foreigners. Although there were also many other servants bought with silver, he showed the loyalty of the servants born in his household. Likewise, Christ did not gather everyone indiscriminately, but those born within the faith. And they proclaimed the True One from the True One, the Living One from the Living One, Light from Light.

What separation would you suppose there is between light and light? What difference between life and life? What distinction between truth and truth? And what is still more remarkable is that the Father is called light. John says, “God is light,” and speaks of the Son with an addition: “He was the true light.” The Father is called simply light, without qualification, because of the assumption, and because the audacious heretics unite [?] against the divinity of the Son, although [?] someone dares to direct hostility against the Father. Nevertheless, the Scriptures make what is evident known in clear words and establish what is doubtful through the truth. The Father is called light without any addition, because the proclamation alone is sufficient to make him known. The Son is also named light. So that you may not suppose that the former is intelligible and essential light, while the latter is some visible and [?] light, he confirms the statement with an addition: “He was,” he says, “the true light.”

Again, so that no one may say, “Just as the sun is light and the moon is light, but one is a great light and the other a small one, so the Father might be some great light and the Son a small one,” Isaiah goes before as a herald and sets this right. He says, “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the River Jordan: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” If the Father is called a great light, behold, the Son too is named a great light. Great is the one who begets, and great is the one begotten; great is the root, and great is the fruit; great is the light, and great is the radiance of the light. I recognize no great and small there, but only greatness. I know the Trinity as one.

Great is the Father, as Jeremiah the prophet says: “You are God, great and eternal.” Paul also says of the Son, “We await the blessed hope and the appearing of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ.” And David says, “Great is the Lord, and great is his power.” Surely he is not one person and his power another? The apostle bears witness that the Son is his power: “Christ,” he says, “the power of God.” Again the prophet says, “Great is our Lord,” as though to say, “Great is the Father, and great is his power—the Holy Spirit,” just as the giver of life said to the apostles, “Stay and remain in Jerusalem until you receive power from on high.”

But see how cleverly the opponents argue. “This,” they say, “is a power that distributes the greatness of the promises, and nowhere is it written that the Spirit is God, but rather that he is the pledge of the inheritance.” Pay attention: a pledge is some part of the gift, not the entire gift, but a part of the whole. “It is written in the Apostle,” they say, “that you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance. Do you see,” they say, “that he is a gift and not God?” Now, if you find the Father also called a portion and an inheritance, will you follow the words there too, rather than their meaning? For an inheritance and a portion are gifts from the giver, and not the giver himself who grants the inheritance. And if calling the Holy Spirit a pledge makes you stumble, then, when you hear of the Father that he is a portion of the inheritance, will you direct your blasphemy against him too? Pay careful attention: he did not say “inheritance,” but “a portion of the inheritance.” David bears witness: “The Lord,” he says, “is the portion of my inheritance.” Therefore, just as he is a portion of the inheritance, so the Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance. If calling the Father a portion of the inheritance makes him lesser, then so does calling the Spirit the pledge of the inheritance. Elsewhere David says, “The Lord is my portion in the land of the living.” A portion is some part of something, not the whole of it. Now, if you hunt for words rather than examine their meaning, nothing will then prevent you from blaspheming the God whom you think you are glorifying. “The Lord,” he says, “is the portion of my inheritance,” and, “The Lord is my portion in the land of the living.” Must we explain why the entire Power is called a portion and an inheritance? Because we worship God by our own free choice, and some take pleasure in foolishness, and some have fallen, he becomes the portion of the believers who choose him. It is something like this: “Let the Levites,” he says, “have no portion of the land, for the Lord is their portion, whom they have chosen.” The prophet makes it clear that he chose God of his own will, and not under compulsion: “The Lord,” he says, “is my portion.” If God loses nothing of his divinity when he is called a portion, then likewise the Holy Spirit loses nothing of his divinity when he is called a pledge.

Let us henceforth put aside this [?] tangled confusion and receive the apostolic faith. How long will you set up scales and weigh the divine words? You have your thoughts as weights in your mind: weigh the Savior’s gifts. Consider which belong to the flesh and which to the divinity, which to his dignity and which to his saving work, so that it may not also be said of you, “In Canaan’s hand are scales, scales of injustice,” and so that the other saying may not apply to you: “The sons of men are vain; they sin in the scales.” You have the beam of the scales, yet you distort the just balance. Be attentive to the balanced weights of the Giver of life; pay attention and look carefully. “I and my Father,” he says, “are one.” Where, then, is the inequality? See the balanced weights of the divine Word: “Whoever has seen me,” he says, “has seen my Father.” Where, then, is the one that tips downward or the one that rises upward? See the Father as liberator, the Son as liberator, and the Spirit as liberator. “Unless the Son sets you free,” he says, “you are slaves.” And Paul says, “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set us free.” Thus the Father sets free, the Son sets free, and the Spirit sets free. But may all of us be freed from the yoke of sins, escape the yoke of the heretics, set our steadfast faith aright, and give glory to the Holy Trinity forever.
